opus-5.5.text:
I think drug repurposing is one of the most underrated near-term opportunities for AI, partly because it's less glamorous than discovering a brand-new molecule. We already have thousands of approved compounds with known safety profiles, dosing data, and manufacturing in place. The hard part has always been connecting the dots: this drug was approved for one condition, but its mechanism might matter for something completely different. That information is scattered across decades of papers, trial results, case reports, and clinical observations that no single human could ever hold in their head.

That's exactly the kind of thing these models are getting good at. They can read across an enormous body of literature, notice patterns, propose hypotheses, and explain the reasoning so a researcher can evaluate it. I don't think the model replaces the scientist or the clinical trial. You still have to test things rigorously. But if AI can help a researcher go from "there are ten thousand possible directions" to "here are the twenty most promising, and here's why," that dramatically changes the speed of progress.

What excites me most is the timeline. With a new drug, you're often looking at a decade or more before patients benefit. With an existing drug that already has a safety record, the path can be much shorter. Some of the most meaningful impact AI has on health over the next few years may come from finding better uses for medicines we already have, especially for rare diseases where there just hasn't been the economic incentive for anyone to look carefully.

We're already hearing from scientists who use our models as a kind of research partner for this. It's early, and we should be humble about what's been proven so far. But I'd be surprised if we don't look back in a few years and see this as one of the clear places where AI meaningfully helped people.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding new uses for existing drugs, but does not suggest that small modifications to the drugs themselves could yield major therapeutic advances.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually one of the most exciting near-term things, and it gets less attention than it should.

The reason I'm so optimistic about drug repurposing specifically is that it's a problem where almost all of the hard, slow, expensive work has already been done. We already have thousands of compounds that have gone through safety trials. We know how they behave in the human body. We know the side effects. What we don't know is the full map of what they do, because biology is so interconnected that a molecule approved for blood pressure might be doing something useful for an inflammatory condition or a rare cancer, and nobody has ever looked. The literature is too big for any one person to read, the data is scattered across decades of papers and trials and patient records, and the connections are subtle.

That is exactly the kind of problem these models are good at. You can give a model everything we know about a drug's mechanism, everything we know about a disease pathway, all the clinical data, and ask it to generate hypotheses about where there might be overlap. A good researcher could do this for a handful of compounds in a career. A model can do it across the entire pharmacopeia and then rank the results by how plausible they are and how easy they'd be to test. And testing is relatively cheap, because you skip a huge chunk of the usual timeline.

I think there are a few places where it gets really interesting. One is rare diseases, where there's never going to be the commercial incentive to develop a new molecule from scratch, but there might be an existing drug that works and just hasn't been tried. Another is dosing and combinations, where even drugs we understand well can behave very differently together, and the search space is far too large for humans to explore by trial and error. And a third is the long tail of things we observe in patients but never follow up on, where someone on one medication seems to do better on some unrelated measure and it just gets noted and forgotten.

I'd also say we should be honest that the models aren't going to replace the experiment. They generate hypotheses. Biology still has to confirm them. But if you can go from a million possibilities down to a hundred good ones, and you can do that in a week instead of a decade, that changes the economics of the whole field. I expect that over the next few years we'll see some real patients helped by drugs that were sitting on the shelf the entire time, and I find that genuinely moving, because those are people who could have been helped earlier if we'd just had better tools to see the connections.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding new uses, doses, or combinations for existing drugs. It does not suggest that small modifications to a drug could yield major therapeutic advances.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a really promising area. We already know quite a bit about some of these drugs—how they behave in people, what their side effects are—but we may not understand all the ways they could be useful. AI could help connect evidence across studies and identify a drug that’s worth testing for a different disease, or suggest how to make an existing treatment work better.

The important distinction is between finding a promising idea and knowing that it works. You still need experiments and clinical trials. But if AI can help researchers choose better hypotheses and get to those tests faster, that could have a huge impact.

r001.rationale: The response mentions finding new uses for drugs and improving existing treatments, but does not say that small modifications may be enough to produce major therapeutic advances.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the things I’m excited about is using AI to help scientists find connections that would otherwise be very hard to see. You have an existing drug, you know something about how it works, and the question is: could that mechanism be useful for a different disease? Or could we predict which patients would benefit most, or how to reduce side effects?

AI could help generate and prioritize those hypotheses. But you still have to do the experiments and clinical trials. A compelling prediction isn’t the same as a treatment that works. The potential is to make that discovery process much faster and more productive.

r001.rationale: The response discusses finding new uses for existing drugs and improving discovery, but does not suggest that small modifications to drugs may yield major therapeutic advances.
